title: Fit a text's cohesion to what readers know
statement: Match how explicit and connected a text is to its readers' knowledge: highly cohesive texts help readers new to a topic but can lower deeper understanding for knowledgeable readers.
detail: The reading project's evidence base lists the interaction of text coherence and prior knowledge in its authoring tier, for designing a ladder of text difficulty (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/skills/reading-science/PRIORITIES.qmd`). Its digest of the RAND Reading Study Group's 2002 report quotes both halves: for readers with little knowledge of the topic, texts with high coherence consistently produced higher scores than texts with low coherence, while for readers with much knowledge a coherent text base slightly enhanced recall but lowered performance on tests that tapped the mental model (`grade3-reading/knowledge_bot/skills/reading-science/DIGEST-rand-mr1465-2002.qmd`, claims 69 and 70, pp. 107-108).

evidence.quote: The coherence x knowledge text-tuning interaction (high-coherence texts help low-knowledge readers; can under-stretch high-knowledge readers on deep measures).
For these readers, texts with high coherence consistently produced higher performance scores than texts with low coherence.
A coherent text base slightly enhanced recall, but actually lowered performance on tests that tapped the mental model.

citations.ref: RAND Reading Study Group 2002, Reading for Understanding (MR-1465)
